blocks.prompt: The Red Truck That Is Really a Pump
blocks.text: A fire truck is a giant toolbox on wheels. Behind the shiny doors are axes, ropes, and a ladder that folds out long. The truck brings its own water in a tank. But the tank runs out fast. So the firefighters hook a fat hose to a fire hydrant on the street. Now the water never stops. A pump inside the truck squeezes the water and pushes it back out hard, so it can shoot up high. One firefighter stays with the truck and works the pump. The rest of the crew takes the hose to the fire.

blocks.prompt: The Truck That Runs Out of Water
blocks.text: A fire engine looks like it brings all the water it needs. It does not. A big red engine carries about 750 gallons in its tank. That sounds like a lot. Fire does not think so. Open one hose line all the way and the tank empties in a few minutes. Aim the big water cannon on the roof of the truck and it empties in under one. So the first job at a fire is not spraying. It is finding water. One firefighter drops off the back with a thick supply hose and runs it to the nearest hydrant. A hydrant is just the top of a pipe that reaches down under the street and joins the whole city's water. It does not run out. Now the engine can do the thing it was built for. Under the shiny paint, a fire engine is really a giant pump. Water arrives from the hydrant slow and gentle, at the same pressure that fills your kitchen sink. The pump squeezes it and shoves it back out, hard enough to reach a second-story window. The tank was never the plan. The tank buys the crew a few minutes. The hydrant does the rest.

4.title: The Red Truck That Is Really a Pump
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Red Truck That Is Really a Pump

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Engine, or pumper: water, hose, pump
Ladder truck: often carries no water
Aerial ladders reach about 100 feet
Outriggers stop the truck tipping over
A tiller truck has two drivers
Hook and ladder: hooks pulled burning walls down

blocks.prompt: Two Trucks, Two Jobs
blocks.text: When people say fire truck, they usually mean one of two very different machines. The first is the engine, also called the pumper. It carries hose, a water tank, and the pump that does the real work. The engine's job is water. It parks near a hydrant, feeds the hose lines, and one firefighter stays behind at the pump panel the whole time, watching gauges and adjusting pressure while everyone else disappears inside. The second is the ladder truck. Many ladder trucks carry no water at all. Where the tank would be, there is an aerial ladder that unfolds to about 100 feet, roughly the height of a ten-story building. Its job is reaching: getting people out of upper windows, getting firefighters onto roofs, and aiming water down from above. Before that ladder goes up, the crew swings out metal legs called outriggers and presses them against the pavement. Without them, the weight of the extended ladder would tip the whole truck over. Some cities use a stranger third version. A tiller truck is built in two pieces, like a semi-trailer, and it has two drivers. One sits up front. The other sits at the very back and steers the rear wheels on their own. It looks like a stunt. It is not. It lets a truck longer than a school bus turn corners on narrow old streets that would trap anything else. The oldest name for a ladder truck is the strangest one: hook and ladder. Long before pumps were any good, the surest way to stop a fire spreading was to pull the burning building down with long hooks and chains, so there was nothing left to burn. The hooks are gone. The name stayed.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A gallon of water weighs about 8 pounds
A loaded engine can weigh 20 tons
The truck's own engine drives the pump
A large pump moves 1,500 gallons a minute
Hand pumps, then steam and horses, then motors
Motor fire engines arrived around 1910

blocks.prompt: A Pump on Wheels
blocks.text: Take away the paint, the ladders, and the noise, and what is left of a fire engine is the thing that actually matters: a pump. Start with the weight, because everything else follows from it. Water is heavy. A single gallon weighs about eight pounds, so the 750 gallons sloshing in an engine's tank add roughly three tons before you count the truck, the hose, the tools, or the crew. A loaded engine can weigh twenty tons or more. That is why fire engines accelerate slowly, brake slowly, and swing around corners like a loaded ship. The siren is not there for drama. It is asking, well in advance, for the room the truck physically needs. Now the pump. It is driven by the truck's own diesel engine, which is a neat trick: when the driver arrives and sets the brake, the engine stops turning the wheels and starts turning the pump instead. The same power that moved twenty tons down the street now moves water. It needs to. A hydrant delivers water at ordinary street pressure, which is fine for filling a bathtub and hopeless for fighting a fire on a third floor. The pump takes that gentle flow and multiplies its pressure, so the water leaves the nozzle with enough force to knock a grown adult off their feet. A large engine can move more than 1,500 gallons every minute, which is why the pump operator never leaves the panel. Too little pressure and the water does not reach. Too much and the hose becomes dangerous to hold. None of this is new. It is very old machinery getting faster. Two hundred years ago a fire engine was a wooden tub with a handle on each side, and the pump was a line of neighbors working those handles until their arms gave out. Then came steam pumpers, hauled by horses, which finally made pressure without human muscle. Then, around 1910, came the motor truck, which made speed. Every version since has been the same argument stated in metal: get water to the fire, get pressure into the water, and do both before the fire wins.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Night vision is sharpest around greenish-yellow
Lime-yellow trucks crash less, red survives anyway
The tank is a head start, not the supply
High-rises: the engine pumps into a standpipe
US departments answer more medical calls than fires
Aerial ladders reach roughly ten stories

blocks.prompt: Red, Loud, and Almost Out of Water
blocks.text: A fire engine is an argument about time, and almost every part of it is there because somebody once lost that argument. Start with the color. Nearly every American fire engine is red, and almost nobody can tell you why. The usual explanation is tradition. Red paint was expensive, so early volunteer companies used it to show off, and the habit hardened into a fact about the world. It may also be wrong. Beginning in the 1980s, an optometrist named Stephen Solomon studied fire truck crashes and pointed out something the human eye makes obvious. In dim light, red is one of the first colors we stop seeing well, because night vision is sharpest around greenish-yellow. Solomon's work pushed some departments to buy lime-yellow trucks, and the studies found those trucks were involved in fewer accidents. Most departments went back to red anyway. A fire truck is not only a machine. It is a symbol people expect to see, and expectation has a value too. Now the water, which is the part everybody gets wrong. The tank on a pumper holds a few hundred gallons. Opened wide, one hose line drains it in minutes, and the water cannon on the roof drains it in under one. The tank is not the supply. The tank is a head start. The real supply is under the street, so the opening minutes of a structure fire are spent solving a plumbing problem: run a wide supply line from the hydrant to the engine, so the pump has something to work with. In a tall building, even that is not enough, because no ladder reaches the twentieth floor. Instead the engine pumps into a standpipe, a dry pipe built into the building itself, and the crew climbs the stairs with folded hose to plug into an outlet near the fire. The building becomes part of the truck. Then there is the ladder, which is not really about ladders. A modern aerial reaches roughly 100 feet, about ten stories, and it rises only after the crew extends the outriggers that stop the truck tipping. What the aerial actually buys is a second path. Firefighters go in through the door, and the ladder gives them a way out through a window. Nearly every design choice on the truck is a version of that idea. Two ways in, two ways out, and a plan for when the first one fails. The strangest fact about the fire truck is what it mostly does now. In the United States, fire departments answer far more medical calls than fires. Smoke alarms, sprinklers, and building codes worked, and the number of fires fell hard. The trucks stayed. So the enormous red machine built to move water pulls up outside a house because somebody's chest hurts, carrying oxygen, a defibrillator, and a crew trained to keep a person breathing until the ambulance arrives. It is a machine designed for one emergency that quietly grew into a machine for all of them, still painted the wrong color, still carrying a tank that runs dry in minutes, still the fastest honest answer anyone has built to the question of what to do when something has gone badly wrong.
